item.title: Tokyo protests after two suspected Russian aircraft violate Japanese airspace
item.description:
Tokyo protests after two suspected Russian aircraft violate Japanese airspace
Japan has protested to Moscow after two suspected Russian aircraft entered Japanese airspace off the country’s southwestern coastByMARI YAMAGUCHI Associated PressNovember 17, 2026, 1:18 AM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
TOKYO -- TOKYO (AP) — Japan said it protested to Moscow on Tuesday after two suspected Russian aircraft entered Japan's airspace off the country's southwestern coast, the latest incident fueling escalating tensions between the neighbors.
Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi told reporters the suspected Russian aircraft violated Japanese airspace for about five minutes early Tuesday near Fukuoka, long enough for Japan to scramble fighter jets and send warnings.
Japan's government lodged "an extremely stern protest" and “strongly” demanded preventive measures be taken, Koizumi said. He did not specify the types of aircraft involved.
“The violation of the Japanese airspace by the Russian aircraft is not only a serious violation of our country's sovereignty, but also a threat to our safety,” Koizumi said. “It is absolutely unacceptable.”
The Russian aircraft flew across the Tsushima Strait, then headed south and flew above the waters between Taiwan and Japan's westernmost island of Yonaguni, Koizumi said.
Taiwan's defense ministry said Tuesday it detected two Russian military planes entering the island's air defense identification zone from the northeast and that the planes flew through airspace east of the island before leaving the zone south of Taitung County in southeastern Taiwan.
The ministry said it “employed joint intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance measures to monitor the situation continuously and responded appropriately.”

item.title: El Salvador's president confirms and celebrates attack on home of key Haitian gang leader
item.description:
El Salvador's president confirms and celebrates attack on home of key Haitian gang leader
El Salvador’s president says that his troops have demolished the lavish home of a prominent gang leader in Haiti known as JeffByDÁNICA COTO Associated PressNovember 18, 2026, 10:35 AM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico -- El Salvador’s president, Nayib Bukele, said Wednesday that his troops demolished the lavish home of a prominent gang leader in Haiti known as Jeff. It wasn’t immediately clear if he was killed.
Bukele posted a video on X that depicts an old video of Jeff posing in front of his mansion in the Caribbean country and then cuts to Salvadoran helicopters flying toward it as they fire shot after shot, with big plumes of smoke rising from Jeff’s home.
“My gift to the Haitian people on the anniversary of the Battle of Vertières,” Bukele wrote.
The 1803 battle was critical in helping secure Haiti's independence from France and transforming it into the world's first Black republic.
It wasn’t immediately known if Haiti’s police and army were involved. A U.N.-backed gang suppression force said that it wasn’t involved.
Jeff is considered one of Haiti's most powerful gang leaders. His real name is Jeff Larose, but he's known as Jeff Canaan, Jeff Gwo Lwa and Taliban. He has long controlled a community known as Canaan in northern Port-au-Prince, leading a gang of an estimated 200 members, according to the United Nations. His so-called Taliban gang based in Canaan is a very close ally of 5 Segond, which has provided it with reinforcements.
Diego Da Rin, a Haiti expert with International Crisis Group, said the attack on Jeff’s home was the obvious next step for Bukele’s operations.
Jeff built the home in mid-2024, complete with a pool emblazoned with his logo.
“It’s very easy to identify it by satellite,” Da Rin said. “It was a very defiant act by him.”

item.title: A Chinese executive is convicted in a case linked to a Bangkok building collapse
item.description:
A Chinese executive is convicted in a case linked to a Bangkok building collapse
A Thai court has found a Chinese executive and Thai shareholders guilty of illegally operating a business in ThailandByJINTAMAS SAKSORNCHAI Associated PressNovember 18, 2026, 10:56 AM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
BANGKOK -- A court in Thailand on Wednesday found a Chinese executive and Thai shareholders of a Thai subsidiary of a Chinese state-owned construction company guilty of illegally operating a business in Thailand in a case related to the collapse of a Bangkok office building last year.
At least 92 people died on March 28, 2025, when an earthquake struck the partially built high-rise, which was to house the State Audit Office. It was the only building in Thailand to collapse completely due to the 7.7-magnitude quake, which was centered in neighboring Myanmar.
The tower was being built by a joint venture between China Railway No. 10 (Thailand) and Italian-Thai Development. Executives from both companies are also facing separate proceedings over alleged wrongdoing related to the building’s collapse.
China Railway No. 10 (Thailand) and its director, Zhang Chuanling, were found guilty of violating Thailand’s Foreign Business Act by using Thai nominee shareholders to conceal the company’s foreign ownership and operating a construction business without the required permission. The Criminal Court in Bangkok fined the company and Zhang 1 million baht ($29,450) each and sentenced Zhang to three years in prison, while also ordering the company to cease operations.
The defendants had denied the charges and were granted bail.
China Railway No. 10 (Thailand) is a Thai-registered affiliate of China Railway No. 10 Engineering Group, part of the Chinese state-owned China Railway group, which operates internationally.

item.title: Nabeel Rajab, prominent Bahraini human rights activist, dies at 62
item.description:
Nabeel Rajab, prominent Bahraini human rights activist, dies at 62
Nabeel Rajab, a prominent democracy activist who advocated for the rights of Bahrain’s Shiite majority and spent years in prison for challenging the country’s monarchy, has diedBySAM METZ Associated Press and ADAM SCHRECK Associated PressNovember 17, 2026, 6:09 AM
Nabeel Rajab, a prominent democracy activist from Bahrain who helped lead the island nation’s 2011 Arab Spring protests and spent years in prison for challenging its monarchy, died on Tuesday. He was 62.
His family found him unresponsive at their home in Turkey on Tuesday morning, friends and activists said. The Bahrain Center for Human Rights, which Rajab once led as president, confirmed his death in a post on X.
“We extend our sincere condolences and heartfelt sympathy to his esteemed family. We pray that God may encompass him with his vast mercy and reward him abundantly for his efforts and contributions,” the group wrote.
Ebrahim Sharif, an activist and close friend of the family, said Rajab's wife and daughter took him to a hospital in Istanbul, where he was pronounced dead. He said after speaking with Rajab's brother that the family believes Rajab likely died of a heart attack.
Rajab for decades was one of Bahrain's leading human rights activists. He frequently posted on social media about Bahrain's treatment of dissidents, and was an unusually visible figure in a country where voicing criticism can carry enormous risk.
In 2002, Rajab helped establish the Bahrain Center for Human Rights, which became a platform for him and his colleagues to call for democratic reforms in the island nation, where a Sunni monarchy rules over a predominantly Shiite Muslim population.
He rose to international prominence in 2011 as the Arab Spring uprisings swept the region and demonstrations erupted in Bahrain.

item.title: Japan urges creation of an Asian energy framework to counter oil crises
item.description:
Japan urges creation of an Asian energy framework to counter oil crises
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has proposed the creation of an Asian energy agency to help countries in the region cope with oil crises, such as the shocks from the Iran warByThe Associated PressNovember 17, 2026, 9:45 AM
MANILA, Philippines -- Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi proposed Tuesday the creation of an Asian energy agency to help countries in the region cope with oil crises, such as the shocks from the Iran war.
Takaichi called for setting up an oil security task force and a Japan-based version of the International Energy Agency for the region. She put forward the plan at a meeting on the sidelines of the annual summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations in the Philippine capital, Manila.
“We would like to position this as an Asian version of the IEA,” Takaichi said.
The IEA is a multigovernmental but independent agency set up in 1974 in response to a severe oil crisis in the early 1970s. It provides policy recommendations and helps to coordinate oil reserves of its members. The Iran war that began in late February has raised the sense of urgency over energy security, especially in Asia.
Japan would help lead an Asian oil security task force, along with the Indonesia-based Economic Research Institute for ASEAN and East Asia, or ERIA, an energy security research organization, to develop rules for emergency releases and sharing of oil from national stockpiles, Takaichi told a meeting of the Asia Zero Emissions Community.

item.title: Pope forgives person who nailed him in the eye with a rosary in Peru
item.description:
Pope forgives person who nailed him in the eye with a rosary in Peru
Pope Leo XIV has forgiven the person who threw a rosary at him before his final Mass in Peru and nailed him in the eyePope forgives person who nailed him in the eye with a rosary in PeruThe Associated PressByNICOLE WINFIELD Associated PressNovember 17, 2026, 3:52 AM
Share
ABOARD THE PAPAL PLANE -- Pope Leo XIV has forgiven the person who threw a rosary at him before his final Mass in Peru and nailed him in the eye, saying it was merely a sign of the person’s profound faith.
Leo got hit during a popemobile ride Monday through the estimated 1.5 million people who had flooded a Lima air base for the service. Leo grimaced and touched his eye but proceeded as if nothing had happened.
During an in-flight press conference en route home, a Peruvian reporter apologized for the incident. Leo, who lived in Peru for two decades and has Peruvian citizenship, brushed it off as merely someone trying to get close to the pope.
And he also joked about it.
“The nice thing about Peruvians, including the person who with a lot of faith simply wanted to offer me a rosary, are things you carry in your heart – or maybe in your eye – but that mark the life of someone,” he said.

item.title: 4 detained in North Macedonia for alleged Iran-backed assassination plot in Greece
item.description:
4 detained in North Macedonia for alleged Iran-backed assassination plot in Greece
Authorities in North Macedonia say four people have been detained for questioning over an alleged Iran-linked assassination plot in neighboring GreeceByThe Associated PressNovember 17, 2026, 10:33 AM
Share
SKOPJE, North Macedonia -- Authorities in North Macedonia have detained four people for questioning over an alleged Iran-linked assassination plot in neighboring Greece, officials said Tuesday.
Bojan Hristovski, director of North Macedonia's domestic security agency, said Tuesday that the suspects are all Macedonian citizens, adding that a fifth person had also been questioned and a sixth remained wanted by the authorities.
Hristovski named one of the Iranian recruiters as Naji Sharifi Zindashti, who is wanted in the United States for allegedly operating a criminal network that targets Iranian dissidents and activists abroad.
He did not give details of the alleged target in Greece, and Greek authorities did not immediately comment on the announcement.

item.title: Pope Leo’s envoy brings message of comfort and unity to Holy Land Christians
item.description:
Pope Leo’s envoy brings message of comfort and unity to Holy Land Christians
The Catholic cardinal who oversees care of the faithful in the Holy Land visited Jerusalem to convey Pope Leo XIV's presence during troubled times for ChristiansByGIOVANNA DELL'ORTO Associated PressNovember 17, 2026, 1:29 PM
JERUSALEM -- The Vatican cardinal who oversees care of the Catholic faithful in the Holy Land visited Jerusalem on Tuesday, saying he wanted to convey the presence of Pope Leo XIV during particularly troubled times for Christians in the region.
Cardinal Claudio Gugerotti, prefect of the Vatican’s Dicastery for the Eastern Churches, prayed before the Holy Edicule inside the Church of the Holy Sepulcher, which marks the site where Christians believe Jesus was buried and rose from the dead.
“Lord, you were here physically,” Gugerotti prayed. “Lord, give hope to the world.”
Leaders of other Christian denominations in Jerusalem listened intently. The incense-filled ceremony, with clergy in solemn robes, offered a show of unity in the basilica where they have sometimes tensely shared worship space in a unique arrangement dating to the 19th century.
Preceded by bagpipers, rows of Franciscan friars and a large cross, Gugerotti and other Christian leaders processed through the narrow stone alleyways of Jerusalem’s Old City to the centuries-old church.
Harassment of clergy and faithful there has been rising. A rare violent attack on a religious sister in April sent shock waves across Israel.
“We know we are not always welcome,” said Sister Marie Reine, a Catholic nun who joined the procession in her white habit. “But our presence can bring peace, too.”
Most of Israel’s Christians are Palestinians, who have been the target of heated rhetoric after Arab-led parties made historic gains in the national elections last month. And neighboring Jordan is reeling from an attack that killed nine worshippers during a service at a Greek Orthodox church.

item.title: Angry crowds rally against Slovakia's pro-Russian leader on Velvet Revolution anniversary
item.description:
Angry crowds rally against Slovakia's pro-Russian leader on Velvet Revolution anniversary
Crowds have gathered in Slovakia to protest the government of pro-Russian Prime Minister Robert Fico on the anniversary of the 1989 Velvet Revolution, which ended communist rule in CzechoslovakiaByThe Associated PressNovember 17, 2026, 1:50 PM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
BRATISLAVA, Slovakia -- People in Slovakia took to the streets Tuesday to rally against the government of pro-Russian Prime Minister Robert Fico on the anniversary of the 1989 Velvet Revolution that brought an end to decades of communist rule in Czechoslovakia.
Opposition parties organized the protests in dozens of communities across the country, where Fico remains as Europe’s most pro-Russian leader since Hungary’s Viktor Orbán was ousted from power in April.
“We’ve had enough of Fico,” chanted people in Bratislava, where organizers estimated 25,000 gathered in the downtown SNP square. One banner had a message for the prime minister: “Go to hell.”
The capital's rally united the liberal groups Progressive Slovakia and the Democrats with pro-business Freedom and Solidarity, the conservative Christian Democrats and an alliance of ethnic Hungarians. Together they hope to defeat Fico and his coalition government in next year’s parliamentary election.
“Just as in 1989, what unites us must be stronger than what divides us,” said Michal Šimečka, leader of the major opposition Progressive Slovakia party. “We’ll win only if we stick together.”
The government angered opponents by sending Foreign Minister Juraj Blanár to Russia for talks about renewing economic cooperation and other ties between the two countries for the first time since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

item.title: Iran war dents Middle East sports as events are canceled. F1 bucks the trend
item.description:
Iran war dents Middle East sports as events are canceled. F1 bucks the trend
The season-ending Formula 1 races in the Middle East are going ahead despite the war in Iran and retaliatory attacks across the region that have canceled or postponed other large sports eventsBySTEPHEN WADE AP sports writerNovember 18, 2026, 12:07 AM
Share
Two season-ending Formula 1 races in the Middle East are going ahead despite the war in Iran and retaliatory attacks across the region that have canceled or postponed other large sports events. This includes two Formula 1 races earlier this year in Saudi Arabia and Bahrain.
The conflict has upended the region's image as a safe haven where governments and sponsors have kicked in billions to lure mega-sports events. This comes as Europe and North America appear wary of such lavish spending.
“The situation could change but the geography will not change,” Sebastian Sons, who follows sports in the Middle East with the German research institute CARPO, told The Associated Press. “The Middle East and the Gulf region are always a volatile and fragile region.”
Going ahead is an endorsement for doing business in the region, but has also prompted concerns about safety from some teams and staff. Mohammed Ben Sulayem, the president of auto racing's world governing body FIA, has said “we are fully prepared” to pull off the two races: Qatar on Nov. 29 and Abu Dhabi on Dec. 6.
Ben Sulayem is from the United Arab Emirates.
A MotoGP race was held in Qatar on Nov. 8 on the track where F1 races. MotoGP is operated by Liberty Media, which also runs F1.
“Holding the races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi signals that those two are stable and able to host large-scale sporting events. It is important they are seen to be open for business,” Kristian Ulrichsen, a political scientist at Rice University's Baker Institute, told The AP.
